extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional law / political science; scholars of American institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the principles and procedures that determine the jurisdiction, independence, and practical operation of the federal courts under the U.S. Constitution, including limits on state power and procedural techniques used to enforce federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of federal judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Their office was made inalienable; and it was determined that their salary, when once fixed, should not be altered by the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges are appointed by the president with the advice of the senate to render them independent of other authorities. The fixed salary and inalienable tenure are presented as safeguards of judicial independence from legislative or executive interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court's right to determine jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme court of the United States was therefore invested with the right of determining all questions of jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid collisions between state and federal tribunals and to form a uniform body of jurisprudence, the Supreme Court was given the authority to decide which cases are federal. This centralization restricts state independence but ensures national uniformity in interpreting federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter and Party are first conditions of federal jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Matter and the Party are the first Conditions of the federal Jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal jurisdiction is determined both by the subject-matter (type of cause) and by the quality of the parties involved. Certain parties (e.g., ambassadors, the Union, states) or certain causes (e.g., maritime, arising under federal law) automatically fall within federal jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambassador suits are federal
rubrics_metrics.description: When an ambassador is a party in a suit, that suit affects the welfare of the nation, and a federal tribunal is naturally called upon to decide it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ambassadors represent foreign nations and such suits implicate national interests, they belong to federal courts regardless of other considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suits to which the Union is a party are federal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union itself may be involved in legal proceedings...the federal courts, therefore, take cognizance of these affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It would be contrary to custom and sense for the Union to be litigated before a tribunal representing another sovereignty; thus cases involving the Union are heard in federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity jurisdiction (citizens of different states)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two parties belonging to two different states are engaged in a suit, the case cannot with propriety be brought before a court of either state...select a tribunal like that of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid bias or suspicion, disputes between citizens of different states are placed before federal courts as a neutral forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-versus-state controversies are federal
rubrics_metrics.description: When the two parties are...states, an important political consideration is added...the quality of the parties...gives a national importance to all their disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversies between states concern the peace of the whole Union and are therefore within federal jurisdiction; historical notes (e.g., Chisholm v. Georgia and subsequent amendment) indicate shifts in how such suits are handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maritime and law-of-nations cases are federal
rubrics_metrics.description: All the questions which concern maritime commerce evidently fall under the cognizance of the federal tribunals...they are connected with the interpretation of the law of nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the sea transcends individual state jurisdiction and maritime issues implicate international law, admiralty and related matters are federal. Examples include piracy and other maritime causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal-question jurisdiction: cases arising under U.S. laws and treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial power of the supreme court shall extend to all cases in law and equity arising under the laws of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a case turns on the interpretation or validity of federal laws or treaties (e.g., state laws conflicting with constitutional prohibitions, disputes over import duties), federal courts have jurisdiction to ensure uniform application of national law.

rubrics_metrics.name: State laws opposed to the Constitution can be appealed to federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the laws of the United States are attacked, or whenever they are resorted to in self-defence, the federal courts must be appealed to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizens injured by state laws that conflict with the Constitution may seek relief in federal courts. Note (American Editor): state courts exercise concurrent jurisdiction and an appeal to federal courts lies only when the state decision is adverse to the federal-law claimant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions on ex post facto laws and impairment of contracts by states
rubrics_metrics.description: The states are prohibited from making ex-post-facto laws in criminal cases; and any person condemned by virtue of a law of this kind can appeal to the judicial power of the Union. The states are likewise prohibited from making laws which may have a tendency to impair the obligations of contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contracts clause protects pre-existing grants/charters and other contract-based rights (e.g., Dartmouth College case). The text discusses scope and examples: state grants accepted by private individuals are contracts that cannot be revoked by later state law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent exercise of jurisdiction by state courts with federal right of appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: By the grant of power to the courts of the United States to decide certain cases, the powers of the state courts are not suspended, but are exercised concurrently, subject to an appeal to the courts of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State courts may decide cases involving federal questions, but federal review is available when a state decision is against the claimant's federal rights (see cited cases and editorial note).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural principle: prefer suing private individuals rather than states to enforce federal law
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators ought to strive as much as possible to bring private individuals, and not States, before the federal Courts...the federal courts...should only take cognizance of parties in an individual capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid direct hostility between federal government and states and to preserve judicial authority in a federation, Americans typically enforce federal law by enabling private citizens harmed by state laws to bring suit, thereby attacking the law's effects indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal courts attack laws in their consequences, not their principle
rubrics_metrics.description: It attacks the law in its consequences, not in its principle, and it rather weakens than destroys it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When federal courts vindicate federal rights against state legislation, they often annul particular effects (e.g., particular titles or grants) rather than directly invalidating the state's law in whole, thereby enervating but not wholly destroying provincial legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: High rank and political influence of the Supreme Court
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme court of the United States is the sole tribunal of the nation...its prerogatives are almost entirely political.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Court decides cases arising under federal laws, treaties, admiralty, and issues affecting the law of nations, and because it sometimes adjudicates disputes between sovereign entities (states), its decisions have broad political consequences; the discretion of a small number of judges can profoundly affect national tranquility and the Union's existence.
